items.statement:
Assume full AC. Take a surface pair and its standard finite intersection arcs satisfying the hypotheses of the balanced-span smooth sphere quotient: the common boundary link is nonempty, there are no closed surface components or intersection circles, both surfaces have $p$ components, and the number of standard arcs equals the sum of their first Betti numbers. Let $Q$ be a continuous ambient surjection with exactly those arc fibers, whose surface image $S=Q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of $p$ spheres and whose every sphere contains the images of exactly one component of each surface. In particular one may take the smooth sphere quotient constructed there.

Then $G=Q(L)\subset S$ is a finite topologically embedded graph, connected on each sphere. Its vertices are the distinct points $Q(A_j)$, each of valence four; components without vertices are circles. At each vertex there is a supplied topological disk chart with four radial graph arms, with the sectors from $Q(F_0)$ and $Q(F_1)$ alternating cyclically. Away from vertices the graph has an ordinary line chart, and each component of $S\setminus G$ belongs to exactly one of the two surface images. This is a topological marked graph assertion; it does not assert that the graph is smooth or specify overcrossings.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty boundary link $L$, no closed components, and supplied radial collars. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ pairwise disjoint isolated smooth arcs $A_j$ with distinct endpoints on $L$. Each is the radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior, and the two transverse boundary-curve crossings at its ends have equal ordered signs on the boundary tori oriented outward toward the exterior. No intersection circles occur. Suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_0;\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_1;\mathbb Z)$.

For every open neighborhood $N$ of $L\cup\bigcup_j A_j$ there is a continuous surjection $Q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off $N$, whose only nonsingleton fibers are exactly the $A_j$, such that $Q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of exactly $p$ smooth embedded two-spheres. Each sphere contains the images of exactly one component of each $F_i$. The assertion allows disconnected or nonorientable spanning surfaces and an empty arc list. It does not assert that $Q$ is smooth, recover an alternating diagram, or identify the quotient graph $Q(L)$ with the original link.

Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty boundary link $L$, with no closed components and with supplied radial collars around $L$. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ pairwise disjoint smooth arcs $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ whose distinct endpoints lie on $L$. Each arc is the isolated radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior; the two boundary curves on the surrounding tori cross transversely at its endpoints, with equal ordered intersection signs when the tori are oriented outward toward the exterior. Thus every arc is standard. No intersection circles occur.

Write $b_i=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_i;\mathbb Z)$ and suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=b_0+b_1$. There is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$ whose only nonsingleton fibers are exactly the arcs $A_j$, supported in any prescribed disjoint neighborhoods of those arcs. Its image $S=q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of exactly $p$ locally flat embedded topological two-spheres. Each component of $S$ contains the images of exactly one component of each $F_i$. The conclusion includes $n=0$ and allows nonorientable or disconnected spanning surfaces. It does not assert smoothness of these quotient spheres or reconstruct a link diagram.

Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a smooth link with chosen disjoint smooth normal tubes, and let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth embedded spanning surfaces with boundary $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily. Supply radial collar coordinates in the tubes in which each surface collar is given by a smooth ray direction depending on the boundary parameter. Put $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu L$, and orient each torus of $\partial\nu L$ as the boundary of the oriented solid tube, so its outward normal points into $X$. Orient the two surface boundary curves on those tori compatibly with $L$.

Let $\alpha$ be a smoothly and properly embedded arc of transverse intersection of $F_0\cap X$ and $F_1\cap X$, transverse to $\partial X$, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially through the supplied collars to the corresponding points of $L$, obtaining a smooth embedded arc $A$. Assume a neighborhood of this extended arc contains no other intersection components. Write $i_0,i_1\in\{1,-1\}$ for the ordered local intersection signs of the two boundary curves at its endpoints, measured on $\partial\nu L$.

The union $F_0\cup F_1$ has a closed intrinsic neighborhood $K$ of $A$ modeled by four pages with common arc, glued at each end by one of the matchings $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$, with pages zero and two on $F_0$ and pages one and three on $F_1$. The two end matchings differ if and only if $i_0=i_1$. Consequently collapsing $A$ in this neighborhood gives a closed topological disk exactly when $i_0+i_1=2$ or $-2$. When $i_0+i_1=0$ it gives two disks joined at their interior centers. For the standard cases the ambient arc-collapse map can be chosen supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $A$, and its image of $K$ is an embedded topological disk. Local flatness of that disk is not asserted here.

Take four rectangles $P_j=[0,1]_t\times[0,1]_r$, $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Identify their edges $r=0$ pointwise in the $t$ coordinate to a common arc $A$. At each end $t=e$, $e\in\{0,1\}$, also identify the radial edges pointwise in $r$ by a matching $\mu_e$, where each $\mu_e$ is one of $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$. Let $K$ be this finite quotient complex, and let $C$ be the image of the four outer edges $r=1$.

If the two end matchings differ, then $K/A$ is a closed topological disk whose boundary is exactly the image of $C$, and the collapsed arc is an interior point of that disk. If the two end matchings agree, then $K/A$ is two closed disks joined at their interior centers, so it is not a topological two-manifold at the collapsed point. Explicitly, $K/A$ is the cone on the graph $C$; the latter is one four-edge circle for distinct matchings and two disjoint two-edge circles for equal matchings.

Consequently, if a finite Hausdorff two-dimensional cell complex is already a topological two-manifold away from finitely many disjoint arc subcomplexes, with neighborhoods modeled by the interiors $r<1$ of these four-page models with distinct end matchings, collapsing those arcs gives a topological two-manifold. No boundary is created at a collapsed point. Collapsing any finite disjoint arc subcomplexes preserves the Euler characteristic, whether or not the local end matchings differ. These are intrinsic topological conclusions; an ambient embedding or local flatness needs separate data.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

derivations.claim: The restriction of $Q$ to $L$ identifies precisely each pair of endpoints of $A_j$. There are no other identifications, because the whole nonsingleton fibers are exactly the disjoint arcs and their interiors miss $L$. Subdivide $L$ at these finitely many endpoints, adding a vertex on a circle with no endpoints for its cell presentation. Its quotient identifies the two distinct endpoints of each arc to one vertex and retains every open edge. Each such vertex has four incident half-edges, two from each original link point, with loops counted twice. The compact quotient maps continuously and bijectively onto Hausdorff $G$, so is a homeomorphism. It is therefore a finite topological graph, with the additional subdivision vertices on vertex-free circles understood as auxiliary.

In the four-page neighborhood [F2], the image of $L$ is exactly the four radial seams: the common arc is the cone center, and the two short boundary intervals at its endpoints give the four rays. Opposite matchings make the outer graph one circle. Its four page edges alternate between the two surfaces, since every successive endpoint identification joins one page from each surface. The coning chart therefore gives a disk with four radial graph arms and alternating surface sectors. At an uncollapsed boundary point the distinct radial collars give the line chart by angular straightening of their two rays. Any two ambient quotient maps with the same arc fibers differ by an ambient homeomorphism: both factor through the same compact quotient, and the induced continuous bijection of Hausdorff compact targets is a homeomorphism. Hence these actual local marked charts transfer to the specified $Q$, including when its later cap maps have not preserved smooth marked curves.

Fix one sphere component $S_a$ and put $X_i=Q(F_i)\cap S_a$, $G_a=G\cap S_a$. Each $X_i$ is connected, being the image of its one original connected surface component. The intersection $X_0\cap X_1$ equals $G_a$: an equality of image points from the two surfaces is either their original common boundary point or a collapsed common arc, whose image also belongs to $Q(L)$. Use the finite CW structure in [F1] and transport it to this quotient as in step 2.1. Then $X_0,X_1,G_a$ are subcomplexes covering $S_a$. The intersection is nonempty, since every original component has a nonempty boundary circle. Their one-skeleta are connected: attaching a cell of dimension at least two cannot join components of a one-skeleton, as its boundary sphere is connected. Thus for any vertices $u,v$ of $G_a$, there are finite integral cellular one-chains $a\in C_1(X_0)$ and $b\in C_1(X_1)$ with $\partial a=\partial b=v-u$.

The chain $a-b$ is a cellular one-cycle in $S_a$. By [F3] it bounds a cellular two-chain $c$. Split $c=c_0+c_1$ by assigning each of its two-cells to a containing $X_i$, assigning common cells to either side. Then $w=a-\partial c_0=b+\partial c_1$ is a one-chain lying in both cellular chain subgroups, hence in $C_1(G_a)$, and $\partial w=v-u$. If $u,v$ belonged to different graph components, the augmentation counting vertices in the component of $u$ would vanish on every graph edge boundary and hence on $\partial w$, but have value $-1$ on $v-u$. This contradiction proves that all graph vertices lie in one component. Every nonempty finite graph component has a vertex in the chosen cell structure, so $G_a$ is connected.

Finally the two closed subcomplexes $X_i$ cover $S_a$ and intersect exactly in $G_a$. In its complement, the sets $X_i\setminus G_a$ are disjoint, relatively closed and also relatively open because each is the other's complement. Thus a connected complementary component lies wholly in exactly one of them. The line and four-arm charts from step 2.1 give the asserted local colored sectors. Repeating the argument on the finitely many spheres proves all conclusions; when a sphere has no arc vertex its connected finite graph is a single original boundary circle. No crossing height or regularity of marked edges beyond these topological charts has been claimed.

boundaries.reason: The common boundary link is nonempty, every original surface component has boundary, and each sphere contains one component from each side.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 includes a sphere with no arc vertices, whose connected marked graph is a single circle.
Step 4.1 proves connectivity on each individual sphere, allowing p=1 or one arc vertex with loop edges.
Step 1.1 counts a loop twice at a valence-four vertex and retains auxiliary vertices on vertex-free circles.
Step 2.1 uses the actual opposite page matchings and marks their four radial seams; distinct arc endpoints are required in the Statement.
The Statement inherits full AC from finite surface cellulation and quotient suppliers; Step 4.1 is finite integral cellular algebra.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the balanced surface quotient and its finite cellulation. The finite marked graph, local page calculation and cellular chain argument introduce no additional choice.

risk_review.notes: The cellular chain argument proves connectedness without assuming the intersection connected. The local marked charts are topological and do not claim smooth graph edges or overcrossing data.

contract.proof_status_evidence: Five actual local proof rows and scoped final checks; independent mathematical review and canonical readiness pending.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Apply [F1] in pairwise disjoint balls $B_j$ inside the prescribed neighborhoods. Compose the finitely many resulting maps. They preserve their respective balls and are the identity outside them, so their supports do not interfere. The composite $q$ is onto, and its nonsingleton fibers are precisely the $A_j$; it induces a homeomorphism from the ambient quotient onto $S^3$, since the quotient is compact and the target Hausdorff. At each collapsed point the entire local image of $F_0\cup F_1$ is the disk in [F1]. Away from the arcs, a point of just one surface has its ordinary smooth disk chart. At a point of $L$ away from arc endpoints, the radial collars give two distinct rays in each normal disk. They are distinct because equality would give a common radial segment not contained in the listed arcs. Locally along a short interval of $L$, choose continuous angular lifts of those two rays. The increasing piecewise-linear angular map sending them to angles zero and $\pi$, linear on each of the two intervening angular intervals, gives a homeomorphism of the normal disk, continuous along the interval and at its center. Thus their two half-sheets form a locally flat disk. These charts cover the image, which is consequently a compact locally flat embedded closed topological surface $S$. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Produce compatible finite cells before computing Euler characteristic. Double each $F_i$ along its boundary using its smooth collar. On the boundaryless double the graph $G=L\cup\bigcup_j A_j$ is a finite embedded regular graph: put vertices at every arc endpoint and at least one on every remaining link circle. The arcs meet the boundary transversely in the original surface boundary charts, and the graph is contained in the interior of the double. Apply [F3] with the whole double as its compact subsurface. Since $L$ lies in the resulting one-skeleton, the triangles on either side of $L$ restrict to a finite cellulation of the original $F_i$, relative to $G$. Refine the two finite subdivisions of each common graph edge to their union, extending a boundary-edge subdivision across each incident triangle by a finite fan. Both cellulations then restrict to the same cells on the actual graph. Glue them using their actual pointwise identification on $G$. The resulting finite disk attachments give a finite CW structure on $K=F_0\cup F_1$: the quotient of the disjoint compact surfaces by these identifications is homeomorphic to their Hausdorff embedded union. No claim of smooth or affine gluing at a vertex is needed. [given, F3, construct]

2.1 For each connected component of either $F_i$, its triangulation has a boundary edge. In a cellular integral two-cycle, the coefficient of the incident triangle must vanish, because that boundary edge has only one incident triangle. Across an interior edge the two incident coefficients differ only by an orientation sign, so vanishing propagates across it. The dual adjacency graph of the triangles is connected: paths between triangle interiors in the connected surface can be perturbed in finitely many local disk or half-disk charts to avoid the finite vertices and to cross edges finitely many times. Hence all coefficients vanish. There are no cells above dimension two, so $H_2(F_i;\mathbb Z)=0$, and all higher homology vanishes as well. Its zeroth homology has rank $p$. Formula [F4] gives $\chi(F_i)=p-b_i$, with no orientability assumption. [step 1.2, F4, construct, algebra]

2.2 Let $k$ be the number of connected components of $K$. It is finite because $K$ is a union of finitely many connected surface components. Every such component contains a component of each $F_i$: any component of either $F_i$ has a boundary circle in the common $L$, and that circle belongs also to a component of the other surface. Thus $k\le p$. Collapsing an arc does not join distinct components, since that arc lies wholly in one component; the images of the finitely many disjoint compact components remain disjoint compact sets. Consequently $S$ also has exactly $k$ components. [given, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The graph $G$ is obtained from the disjoint link circles, whose Euler characteristic is zero, by attaching the $n$ arc edges at existing vertices, allowing further subdivisions without changing the count. Thus $\chi(G)=-n$. The compatible cell structures in step 1.2 count cells of $G$ twice in $F_0$ and $F_1$ and once in their union. Therefore $\chi(K)=\chi(F_0)+\chi(F_1)-\chi(G)=2p-b_0-b_1+n=2p$. Each $A_j$ is an arc subcomplex, and the compact surface image $S$ is exactly their quotient in $K$. By [F2] it has a finite CW structure with $\chi(S)=\chi(K)=2p$. [given, step 1.2, step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Each component $S_a$ is a connected compact boundaryless topological surface by step 1.1. Its type in [F5] has Euler characteristic at most two, with equality only for the sphere. Explicitly the sphere digon has two vertices, one paired edge and one face, giving two; the genus-$g$ one-face polygon has one vertex and $2g$ edges, giving $2-2g$; the $k'$-crosscap polygon has one vertex and $k'$ edges, giving $2-k'$. These finite polygonal counts agree with the finite cell count of $S_a$ by [F4]. Combining the component inequalities and step 3.1 gives $2p=\sum_a\chi(S_a)\le2k\le2p$. Equality forces $k=p$ and $\chi(S_a)=2$ for every $a$. Thus all $S_a$ are spheres. Since each component already contains at least one component of each $F_i$ and there are exactly $p$ available on each side, it contains exactly one of each. All local-flatness and support assertions were proved in step 1.1; for $n=0$ the same proof uses the identity map and an empty collapse list. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, F4, F5, algebra] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual finite compatible cells from Proof 1.2 and collapse count from Proof 3.1 give finite CW subcomplexes for both surface images and their common marked graph.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Orient $\alpha$ from its first to its second endpoint, and extend this orientation to $A$. Along its open part choose continuous smooth transverse directions $u$ on $F_0$ and $v$ on $F_1$ so that the ordered triple $(\dot A,u,v)$ has positive ambient orientation. Such choices exist along an interval: choose the first direction in finite surface charts and interpolate consecutive signs consistently, and choose the sign of the second by the displayed orientation condition. Inside the radial collars these directions extend to nonzero boundary-tangent directions at the two points of $L$. To verify this, write the two collars as $(s,r,\theta_k(s))$. At a common radial arc their transverse tangents have base component $\partial_s$ and angular component $r\theta_k'(s)$ in the oriented unit angular direction of the normal disk. The boundary-curve transversality says $\theta_0'(s)-\theta_1'(s)\ne0$ there. Hence the orientation of their ordered transverse pair has constant nonzero sign for every $r>0$ and has a definite limiting sign choice on each copy of the boundary tangent at $r=0$. The individual directions remain transverse to $A$ on their own surfaces all the way to those endpoints. [given, construct]

2.1 These directions give relative strips on both surfaces. Extend the transverse field on each surface to a neighborhood of $A$, tangent to $L$ at its two ends, using finitely many surface charts and cutoffs. In the boundary charts take its restriction to $L$ to be a signed unit tangent for a common arclength parameter. Its short flow in [F1] sends $(t,r)$ to the time-$r$ point starting at $A(t)$; the two derivatives are independent on the zero section. By [F1], compactness and the same converging-collision argument as for a normal arc chart, it is an embedded rectangle for a sufficiently small uniform width. Uniqueness of the flow retains its two end edges on $L$. The positive and negative halves give two pages on each surface. By the isolated-intersection hypothesis, after shrinking they meet only along $A$ and their end edges on $L$. Their widths on these end edges can be chosen equal in the common arclength parameter, so the end identifications are pointwise in the page radius. Label the $u$-positive, $v$-positive, $u$-negative and $v$-negative pages by $0,1,2,3$. This gives exactly the asserted four-page neighborhood. [step 1.1, F1, construct]

3.1 At either exterior endpoint project $u,v$ to its boundary torus along $\dot A$. These are nonzero tangent vectors parallel respectively to the two boundary curves: each surface tangent plane contains $\dot A$ and its boundary-curve tangent. Let $s_0,s_1\in\{1,-1\}$ record whether those projected directions agree with the chosen orientations of the respective boundary curves. Following the radial collars to $L$ retains precisely these signs relative to the common oriented boundary tangent, by the collar coordinates in step 1.1. The positive page on $F_0$ is therefore glued to the positive page on $F_1$ exactly when $s_0s_1=1$. If the product is negative it is glued to the negative page instead. Thus the matching at that endpoint is $M$ for product $1$ and $N$ for product $-1$. This assertion uses the signs separately at each endpoint, not a presumed orientation of either whole surface. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 At the first endpoint $\dot A$ points from the solid tube into $X$; at the second it points back toward the solid tube. Projection along $\dot A$ consequently carries the oriented transverse plane determined by $(\dot A,u,v)$ to the oriented torus plane with sign $+1$ at the first endpoint and $-1$ at the second. Indeed the solid tube boundary orientation is defined by putting its outward normal first, and that normal has respectively positive and negative component along $\dot A$. Therefore the two local boundary intersection signs are $i_0=s_0^{\mathrm{first}}s_1^{\mathrm{first}}$ and $i_1=-s_0^{\mathrm{second}}s_1^{\mathrm{second}}$. By step 3.1 the end matchings differ exactly when the two products differ. These displayed formulas show this is equivalent to $i_0=i_1$. Equal matchings occur exactly when $i_0=-i_1$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Apply [F2] to the actual neighborhood in step 2.1. By step 4.1 the standard sign sums $2$ and $-2$ give its disk quotient, while sum zero gives the two-disk wedge. To realize the former quotient inside the ambient sphere use [F3] on the smooth arc $A$, with any prescribed neighborhood as support. Its restriction to the compact $K$ has exactly the same identifications as $K/A$. The induced map of that quotient onto its image in $S^3$ is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism. Its image is therefore an embedded topological disk. The construction has proved its intrinsic topology and its ambient embedding, while making no local-flatness conclusion at the collapsed point. [step 2.1, step 4.1, F2, F3, construct] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual page coordinates identify opposite Fi pages and different-surface endpoint gluings, giving alternating colors on the four-edge outer circle.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 The graph $C$ has four edges, each the parameter interval $t\in[0,1]$ of one page. At $t=0$ its edge endpoints are identified in the two pairs of $\mu_0$, and at $t=1$ in the two pairs of $\mu_1$. Each resulting vertex has degree two. If $\mu_0=M$ and $\mu_1=N$, follow page zero from zero to one, page three back to zero, page two to one, and page one back to zero. This traverses all four edges and returns to the start, so $C$ is a four-edge circle. Reversing the end roles gives the same conclusion when the matchings are interchanged. If both equal $M$, the two circles use page pairs $(0,1)$ and $(2,3)$; if both equal $N$, they use $(0,3)$ and $(1,2)$. Thus the listed cases are exhaustive and identify the whole graph. [given, construct]

2.1 Send the point $(t,r)$ on page $j$ to $([t,j],r)$ in the cone $(C\times[0,1])/(C\times\{0\})$. The end identifications are precisely those already present in $C$, and all points of the common arc $A$ map to the cone point. The map therefore factors continuously through $K/A$. For $r>0$ it identifies exactly the prescribed radial-edge pairs, and at $r=0$ it identifies exactly the collapsed arc. It is consequently a bijection. The domain is compact, being a quotient of finitely many compact rectangles. The target is Hausdorff: a finite graph admits its usual edge-length metric, and its cone is a finite triangular cell complex, or explicitly the finitely many triangles obtained by coning its edges. Hence this continuous bijection is a homeomorphism. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The cone on a polygonal circle is a closed disk: send its consecutive edges to the sides of a convex polygon, and extend each edge map linearly along cone radii to the polygon center. In the two-edge case subdivide each edge once before using this construction. This realizes the distinct-matching case as one disk with boundary $C$ and the cone point in its interior. In the equal-matching case the two components of $C$ give two such disks with only their cone centers identified. This is a Hausdorff wedge, for instance with distance between different disks defined as the sum of their distances to their common center. Every sufficiently small neighborhood of that center contains points of both disks, while deleting the center separates the two parts. A disk or half-disk neighborhood would have connected punctured interior, so no manifold chart can exist there. This proves both local alternatives. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, contradiction]

4.1 In the global cell complex the finitely many disjoint modeled neighborhoods can be taken disjoint. Their quotients have the disk charts in step 3.1. Away from the collapsed arcs the quotient is locally the original space: each arc is a closed subcomplex, so a point off their union has a neighborhood avoiding that union, on which no identification occurs. The quotient remains Hausdorff. Indeed its only nonsingleton equivalence classes are finitely many disjoint closed compact arcs; two distinct classes have disjoint neighborhoods avoiding all the other classes, and for a class that is an arc one may choose a neighborhood containing the entire arc. The resulting neighborhoods are saturated, so separate the quotient classes. Thus the disk charts and the retained original charts make the quotient a topological two-manifold, with no new boundary at the centers. [given, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Finally retain the finite open cells not lying on a collapsed arc and compose their attaching maps with the quotient. Replace each arc's finite zero- and one-cells by one zero-cell. This describes a finite cell structure on the quotient: cell interiors off the arcs remain unchanged, and their boundary maps simply make the prescribed identifications. If an arc has $v$ vertices and $e$ edges in its given subdivision, then $v-e=1$, since it is a subdivided interval. Its replacement changes the Euler count by $1-v+e=0$. Summing over the finitely many disjoint arc subcomplexes shows Euler characteristic unchanged. This calculation is valid for either end-pairing case and also for an empty collection of arcs, when the quotient is the identity. It proves the stated global and Euler assertions without an ambient local-flatness assumption. [given, step 4.1, algebra] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual cone map carries boundary end seams to four radial graph arms in the disk.

current_consumer_trace.next_required_use: Smooth the marked graph on each quotient sphere and recover crossing balls with original link isotopy. No diagram reconstruction or full original flyping acceptance.
